headline: “Friendship” is a learned borrowing from Chinese, first attested in 1900.

sources.quote: Appears to be a learned borrowing from Chinese 友好 (yǒuhǎo). First attested in 1900.

headline: “To feel” was once “to do a feeling”, a verb in a different conjugation.

sources.quote: Shift from 感ずる (kanzuru), a compound of 感 (kan, “feeling”) + する (suru, “to do, to be”). Natural progression from サ行変格活用 (sa-gyō henkaku katsuyō, “s-irregular conjugation”) verbs ending in -uru to 上一段活用 (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: A novel is a “small narrative” — and Wiktionary is still asking who coined it.

sources.quote: From 小 (shō, “small”) + 説 (setsu, “narrative, story”).

headline: The Chinese “time interval” was repurposed in 1881 to translate the philosophers' “time”.

sources.quote: Probably originally borrowed from Middle Chinese compound 時間 (dzyi kɛn, literally “time interval”). Repurposed in the early Meiji period as a translation of the western term time in relation to philosophy in the 1881 publication of 哲学字彙 (Tetsugaku Jii, “Philosophy Dictionary”) compiled by Inoue Tetsujirō. The meaning "hour" can be analyzed as a compound of 時(じ) (ji, “o'clock”) + 間(かん) (-kan, time interval suffix). Compare other terms formed with the suffix 間(かん) (-kan) like 三(さん)分(ぷん)間(かん) (sanpunkan) and 三日(みっか)間(かん) (mikkakan).

The reading is a mix of the goon reading ji and the kan'on reading kan, suggesting either that the reading changed after borrowing (from the expected goon pronunciation of jiken or the expected kan'on pronunciation of shikan), or that this term was independently coined in Japanese after the constituent terms 時(じ) (ji) and 間(かん) (kan) were borrowed.

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: “Many” is in The Tale of the Heike — and its origin is unknown.

sources.quote: First appears in The Tale of the Heike (c. late 12th century).
Origin unknown, kanji spelling appears to be phonetic ateji (当(あ)て字(じ))

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: East-West came from Chinese — and the 西 voices from さい to ざい.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 東西 (MC tuwng sej).
The sai reading for 西 changes to zai as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

meaning: to be burdened with; to carry on (one's) back or shoulder(s)
headline: To shoulder a burden is, literally, to “carry on the back”.

sources.quote: Compound of 背 (se, “back”) + 負う (ou, “to carry or bear something”).
First cited in the early 1200s.

headline: デモ is a clipped デモンストレーション, and Korean has a form 데모 to compare.

sources.quote: Shortening of デモンストレーション (demonsutorēshon). Also see Korean 데모 (demo).

nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: “Preceding” is “go before” — and the same spelling has a native reading, sakiyuki, from 1678.

sources.quote: Ultimately from Middle Chinese 先行 (MC sen haeng, literally “preceding + to go”).
First cited to a text from 833.

headline: “Splendid” is “seeing” plus “thing”, first cited in 1309.

sources.quote: Compound of 見 (mi, “seeing”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 見る (miru, “to see, to look at”)) + 事 (koto, “fact, event, abstract thing”).
First cited to a text from 1309.

headline: “A way of doing” is built from the stem of する and “method”.

sources.quote: From し (shi, “to do”, continuative form of する) + 方(かた) (kata, “method”).

headline: A vase is a “flower jar” in Chinese — and a native reading of the same spelling used an “earthenware pot”.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 花 (MC xwae) and 瓶(びん) (bin, “jar”).

headline: The “stomach” was a deliberately indirect word for “belly”, spelled with a character that means something else.

sources.quote: Compound of 御 (o-, honorific prefix) + 中 (naka, “insides; innards, stomach”). Originally coined as a deliberately indirect 女房詞 (nyōbō kotoba, “woman's word”) for 腹 (hara, “belly, gut”).

The use of the 腹 character to spell 中 (naka) appears to be a relatively recent shift; many dictionaries still list 御中 or お中 as the standard spelling for this term, but usage trends clearly show that this お腹 spelling is now more common for the belly senses.

headline: Gravity borrowed an old Chinese word for “heavy strength” and repurposed it to translate a Dutch one.

sources.quote: Initially from Middle Chinese 重力 (MC drjowngX lik, literally “considerable; heavy + force, power”).
The gravity sense was a repurposing of the older term (the considerable strength sense) as a calque of Dutch zwaartekracht to translate Dutch works as part of Rangaku studies.

headline: “Ugly” is, word for word, “hard to look at”.

sources.quote: Compound of 見(み) (mi, “seeing, looking”, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 見(み)る (miru, “to see, to look at”)) + 難(にく)い (nikui, “hard to do, difficult”), with a literal meaning of “hard to look at” or “difficult to see”.

headline: A lighter and a writer are the same word in katakana.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English lighter.
Borrowed from English writer.

headline: “Usually” was written 不断 first — the kanji we use now were fitted to the sound.

sources.quote: The kanji spelling is phonetic ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)); originally written as 不断(ふだん) (fudan).

headline: “New” began as “freshly coming into being”.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Attested in the Man'yōshū, completed in 759.

Derived as a compound of 新 (ara, from 生る (aru, “to come into being”), cognate also with 有り (ari, “to exist”, the Old and classical Japanese copula), 現れる (arawareru, “to appear, to become manifest”), 荒 (ara, “rough, unfinished”), numerous other terms) + た (ta, suffix indicating state). The core meaning seems to have been "freshly coming into being", and by extension, new.

meaning: to try one's best, to try hard, to persist
headline: “Do your best” once meant “be stubborn” — and the 頑 may belong to neither candidate origin.

sources.quote: Derivation uncertain. The two leading theories are:
* Sense shift from 眼張る (ganbaru, “to keep watch on something, to stare at something”, literally “keep one's eye on something”)
* Shift in pronunciation from 我に張る (ga ni haru, literally “to stick to one's desires, to insist on one's point of view”)
The sense was originally to be stubborn, to be obstinate, with negative overtones. The modern positive sense of to persist, to endure has arisen since the end of the Edo period in 1868.

The spelling is ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)), using the 頑 (gan) character to express a sense of stubborn. The historical kana spelling ぐわんばる (gwanbaru) comes from the use of this 頑 character, and is not related to either of the expected derivations above.
Some sources use both 頑張る and 眼張る as spellings for the persist, endure sense. Other sources split these out as entirely separate entries.

headline: A fountain pen is a “ten-thousand-year pen”.

sources.quote: 万年 (mannen, “ten thousand years; eternity”) + 筆 (hitsu, fude, “pen”)

headline: A pocket notebook is a “hand ledger”, in use from the early 1600s.

sources.quote: Compound of 手 (te, “hand”) + 帳 (chō, “notebook, ledger”). Appears from the early 1600s.

headline: “Enormous” is “swell” plus “big”, and the word is first attested in 1872.

sources.quote: First attested in 1872. Likely a coinage in Japan of Middle Chinese-derived components, as a compound of 膨 (bō, “swell, distend”) + 大 (dai, “big”). The second sense of huge is likely a replacement spelling for Chinese-derived homophone 厖大 (bōdai), first cited to 1898.

meaning: to be dented, to be indented
headline: To be dented is to have “lessened inward” — herikomu worn down to hekomu.

sources.quote: /herikomu/ → /hekomu/

Contraction of 減りこむ (herikomu), itself a compound of 減り (heri, “lessening, becoming less”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 減る heru, “to reduce, to become less”) + 込む (komu, “to go inwardly”).

headline: A truck has a twin in トロッコ, and a running track shares its spelling.

sources.quote: From American English truck. Doublet of トロッコ (torokko).
From English track.

headline: A fault is a “lacking point”, borrowed from Chinese.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese compound 缺點 (MC khwet temX, literally “deficient, lacking” + “point, spot”).

headline: “Perhaps” is a clipped phrase whose first half is still being argued over.

sources.quote: Sources are agreed that modern osoraku as an adverb is a clipping of older noun phrase 恐らくは (osoraku wa), trimming off the topic particle は (wa). This clipped form first appears in the late 1500s. Speculatively, this usage might have been influenced by the -ku adverbial ending used for adjectives.
Past there, different sources give different derivations for the osoraku portion itself.

* May be from the -ku nominalization of verb 恐る (osoru, “to fear, to be afraid of”), originally a 四段活用 (yodan katsuyō, “quadrigrade-conjugation”) verb. In the traditional analysis, the く (ku) noun-forming suffix attaches to the 未然形 (mizenkei, “irrealis form”) of the verb stem, ending in -a: osoru (plain form) → osora- (irrealis) + -ku (noun-forming suffix) = osoraku.

* Older documents also record a form 恐るらくは (osoruraku wa), which may be from 恐る (osoru, “to fear, to be afraid of”) as either a 上二段活用 (kami nidan katsuyō, “upper bigrade-conjugation”) or 下二段活用 (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade-conjugation”) verb. In the traditional analysis, for bigrade verbs, the く (ku) noun-forming suffix manifests instead as らく (raku) and attaches to the 終止形 (shūshikei, “terminal or predicative form”) of the verb, the standard "plain" or "dictionary form" ending in -u: osoru + -raku = osoruraku.

The irregularities in the verb form required for -ku nominalization, and the shifts between bare -ku and longer form -raku, can be resolved if the underlying form of the nominalizing suffix were -aku instead, syntactically acting as a noun, and thus requiring that the verb be in the 連体形 (rentaikei, “adnominal form”). Also, Old Japanese did not allow hiatus (consecutive vowels without an intervening consonant), forcing either vowel fusion or vowel elision. For bigrade osoru, we would have adnominal form osoruru + suffix -aku, with the final -u in osoruru eliding to give us attested osoruraku.
*/osoruru aku wa/ → /osoruraku wa/ → /osoraku wa/ → /osoraku/

meaning: -- honorific form of 食べる (たべる) and 飲む (のむ) --
headline: An honorific “eat” is “take” plus “rise up” — each already honorific.

sources.quote: Compound of 召し (meshi, “taking”, stem of Old Japanese honorific verb mesu, “to see, to look at”, by extension an honorific for “to take, to eat”) + 上がる (agaru, “to rise”, used honorifically to mean “to take up, to eat”).

headline: The newspaper is a Chinese “new hearing” — and in Japanese it began as a clipping of “newspaper paper”.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 新聞 (MC sin mjun). Compare Hokkien 新聞 /新闻 (sin-bûn).
Originally clipping of 新聞紙 (shinbunshi)

headline: “Word” is an old “word” plus an “edge” — and the 葉 in the spelling is only a stand-in.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 言葉 (ko₂to₂ba), attestable since at least the Man'yōshū of 759 CE. In turn, reconstructed as deriving from Proto-Japonic *kətənpa.
Compound of 言(こと) (koto, “word”) + 端(は) (ha, “edge, beginning, end”). The ha changes to ba as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

The term 言(こと) (koto) was formerly the main term for word in Japanese. This term is also cognate with 事(こと) (koto, “thing, fact, event”). The ha may have been added to differentiate from 事(こと) (koto).
The 葉 spelling is an example of ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)).

headline: Geta are “lower clogs” — and the “footwear” sense of 駄 may exist only in Japan.

sources.quote: A surface analysis suggests a Japanese coinage of Middle Chinese-derived components, as a compound of 下(げ) (ge, “lower, under”) + 駄(た) (ta, “loading, carrying; footwear”).

Historical usage suggests a shift from older term 足(あし)駄(だ) (ashida, “clogs”, later, referring more specifically to “tall clogs” in contrast to the “short clogs” referenced by the term 下(げ)駄(た) (geta)), itself deriving from 足(あし) (ashi, “foot”) + 板(いた) (ita, “board”), from the even older practice of wearing flat pieces of wood on one's feet when working in the paddies to keep from sinking into the mud, similar in principle to snowshoes. This latter footwear persisted in use into the 20th century as 田(た)下(げ)駄(た) (tageta, literally “paddy geta”).

The historical derivation indicates that the 駄 character's “footwear” sense, which is specific to Japanese and is not found in Chinese sources, could have arisen from phonetic ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)) usage in the terms 足(あし)駄(だ) (ashida) and 下(げ)駄(た) (geta).

headline: A snowstorm is a verb's stem — and the spelling was borrowed from Chinese for its meaning.

sources.quote: The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of verb 吹雪く (fubuku, “to blow violently (said of wind); to blow a snowstorm”).
The kanji spelling is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)), borrowed from Chinese 吹雪 (chuīxuě).
